**Molecular mechanisms of resistance to Pirimiphos-methyl in *Anopheles gambiae* and *Anopheles coluzzii* from Côte d'Ivoire**

1Department of Vector Biology, Liverpool School of Tropical Medicine, Pembroke Place, Liverpool, L3 5QA, UK.

\*Corresponding author: Email: [Sanjay.Nagi@lstmed.ac.uk](mailto:Sanjay.Nagi@lstmed.ac.uk)  
**Keywords**: RNA sequencing, Anopheles, Insecticide resistance, Transcriptomics

# **Abstract**

Resistance to pirimiphos-methyl, an organophosphate widely used for indoor residual spraying, threatens malaria vector control, yet apart from the *Ace1*-G280S target-site mutation its molecular basis is poorly understood. We sequenced transcriptomes of survivors and unexposed controls (four replicates per group) from sympatric *Anopheles gambiae* and *Anopheles coluzzii* in Bouaké, Côte d'Ivoire, where mortality in F1 progeny exposed to 0.25% pirimiphos-methyl was 34% and 81% respectively. In *An. gambiae* survivors, the cytochrome P450 genes *CYP6M2*, *CYP6M3* and *CYP6M4*, the carboxylesterases *COEAE3G* and *COEAE7G*, and *SAP2* were overexpressed, and ABC transporters and cuticular proteins were enriched. In *An. coluzzii*, enriched categories were dominated by odorant-binding proteins. *Ace1*-G280S was at high frequency in all field cohorts and increased in survivors of both species, whereas resistance alleles at *Gste2* differed between species. The ABC transporter gene *ABCH1* was overexpressed in survivors of both species and lies at a selective sweep in West African *An. coluzzii*, in which a single swept haplotype is found across Burkina Faso, Mali, Ghana and Côte d'Ivoire. The 2Rb inversion was less frequent in surviving *An. coluzzii*. We also detected the sodium channel mutation F1529C, equivalent to the pyrethroid-resistance mutation F1534C in *Aedes aegypti*, on the 402L/1527T haplotype. Resistance to pirimiphos-methyl in Bouaké involves both target-site and expression changes, and the two species differ in their transcriptional response.

# **Introduction** 

Pirimiphos-methyl is an organophosphate insecticide widely-used in indoor residual spraying (IRS) campaigns to target malaria vectors , especially Anopheles gambiae s.l. After long-lasting insecticide bed-nets (LLINs), IRS is the vector control tool with the most evidence available for malaria control programmes, and with resistance to pyrethroids ubiquitous in wild populations (the main compound in LLINs), it is vital that active ingredients for indoor residual spraying formulations are deployed in a way that ensures they continue to work effectively. Actellic 300CS is the main pirimiphos methyl formulation used for IRS, and is usually highly effective and has long residual performance (Dengela et al. 2018; Sherrard-Smith et al. 2018). However pirimiphos-methyl resistance is increasingly reported especially in West Africa, but also in west-central and occasionally East Africa, With alternatives, most notably clothianidin-based formulations now available and in regular use, but a need to preserve as many functional insecticides as possible for resistance management, it is vital not only to identify emergence of phenotypic resistance, but also its underlying mechanisms to understand potential cross-resistance.

As with carbamates, all organophosphates block the action of the acetylcholinesterase enzyme (AChE), encoded by the *Ace1* gene in mosquitoes via competitive binding to its active site. In flies, such as *Drosophila*, *Lucilia*, and *Musca*, multiple target site mutations are found, which can act together, sometimes along with gene copy amplifications, to produce high levels of OP resistance. In mosquitoes, far fewer target site mutations are found, with only a single variant common, which substitutes the ancestral (wild-type) glycine allele for serine at position 119 (G119S; or G280S using *An. gambiae* codon numbering, which we adopt subsequently). The serine allele confers both carbamate and OP resistance but has poor enzymatic efficiency and so carries significant fitness costs. In *Culex pipiens*, duplications of the Ace1 gene involve tandem pairing of resistant and wild type alleles, yielding resistance at a much reduced fitness cost, and these heterogeneous duplications have gradually replaced single copy resistant alleles. In *An. gambiae* heterogeneous mutations are found, but homogeneous duplications which involve multiple copies of resistant alleles with no wild type also occur. These duplicates result in different resistance levels and associated fitness costs, with a general rule that more resistant alleles generate higher levels of resistance, but at a higher fitness cost in the absence of an insecticide. In *An. gambiae* s.l, the *Ace1*\-G280S, mutation in combination with gene duplication, via a haplotype that evolved in *An. gambiae* and introgressed into its sibling species, *An. coluzzii* (Grau-Bové et al. 2021\) confers resistance to organophosphates and carbamates (Djogbénou et al. 2009; Grau-Bové et al. 2021). 

Other physiological mechanisms of resistance to organophosphates remain relatively poorly understood in mosquitoes. In Latin America, the Cyp6 subfamily of P450 genes have been linked to resistance to the organophosphate larvicide temephos in *Aedes aegypti* (Grisales et al. 2013). Yet overall the role of P450s in OP detoxification is unclear; P450-based metabolism is known to convert OPs from their non-insecticidal state to their activated oxon form, but a different metabolism pathway, also P450-mediated, can cause their breakdown (Yunta et al. 2019). Key pyrethroid-metabolising Anopheles Cyp6 P450 including Cyp6M2 and several Cyp6P genes are capable of metabolizing OPs in vivo, including p-methyl. Whether the net result of these reactions is activation or breakdown generally remains unclear (Yunta et al. 2019), although Cyp6M2 overexpression in *An. gambiae* has been shown to result in increased susceptibility to malathion, likely as a result of conversion to the toxic malaoxon metabolite. Esterases, which may sequester activated oxon metabolites to reduce the amount reaching the target site, have also been identified as involved in OP resistance. A series of studies in *Culex pipiens* in southern France linked frequency changes in a duplicated pair of alpha-esterase genes to temephos resistance, with subsequent worldwide spread of the duplication mutation (Raymond et al. 2001). Recently the orthologous pair of alpha-esterases (*Coeae1f* and *Coeae2f*) in *An. gambiae s.l.* have been identified as being under selection, with a gene duplication conferring pirimiphos-methyl resistance in West African *An. gambiae [(Nagi et al., 2024\)](https://paperpile.com/c/S8IWm4/TTx5)*. An alpha-esterase gene has also been associated with temephos resistance in *Aedes aegypti* and *Ae. albopictus* in Latin America (Poupardin et al. 2014; Grigoraki et al. 2015).

Cote D’Ivoire is a hotspot in Africa for the emergence of insecticide resistance in *An. gambiae* and *An. coluzzii* (Edi et al. 2014; Oumbouke et al. 2020). In this study, we perform high-coverage RNA-Sequencing on *An. coluzzii* and *An. gambiae* in Bouaké, central Côte D’Ivoire, a site with confirmed resistance to pirimiphos-methyl in both species Pirimiphos-methyl (REF).

# **Results**

**Sample collections and phenotypic resistance**  
A total of over 450 blood-fed females were collected using prokopack aspirators from the three villages sampled, yielding 60 families for *An. coluzzii*, and 17 families for *An. gambiae*. The limited number for *An. gambiae* was due to an unexpectedly high proportion of *An. funestus* catches in villages which had previously been *An. gambiae*\-dominated (Oumbouké, personal observation). We performed bioassays on F1 progeny. *An. gambiae* bioassay tests showed 34% mortality with 0.25% pirimiphos-methyl (N=150 tested) compared to 81% mortality (N=247 tested) in *An. coluzzii* (Figure 1A), with overall control mortality of 1%. Considering the species mixtures in the field, these results are entirely consistent with the field bioassay results obtained for *An. gambiae s.l.* (Oumbouké et al. unpublished data) and demonstrate a high prevalence of resistance in *An. gambiae* and more moderate, but still confirmed (i.e. \<90%) pirimiphos-methyl resistance in *An. coluzzii*. We performed RNA-Sequencing on 4 biological replicates of unexposed controls and PM survivors of both *An. gambiae* and *An. coluzzii*, alongside the two lab-susceptible strains Kisumu (*An. gambiae*) and Ngousso (*An. coluzzii*).

**RNA-Sequencing and analysis**  
We sequenced the RNA-Sequencing libraries to a high depth, processing 1.463 billion reads in total across the 24 samples. After adaptor removal, 1.254 billion reads were successfully aligned with Kallisto to the AgamP4 reference transcriptome, providing an overall alignment rate of 85.71% (+/- 0.27% standard error). Following read counting with Kallisto, we normalised count data and performed a principal components analysis (Figure 1B) to examine the overall relationships between samples. Samples from each treatment group cluster together, supporting robust replication between biological replicates, and distinct phenotypes between treatment groups. PC1 explained 28.4% of the variance in gene expression and broadly split the lab susceptible strains from the Bouaké field strains. PC2 accounted for 13.3% of the variance and separated *An. gambiae* strains from *An. coluzzii*. Differential expression was performed with DESeq2. 

**Gene-set enrichment analysis**

To identify broader functional patterns linked to pirimiphos-methyl survival, we performed gene-set enrichment analysis (GSEA) across Gene Ontology (GO) terms, PFAM protein domains, and KEGG pathways. This approach allows us to detect coordinated changes in functionally related gene families and pathways, which can provide mechanistic insights into insecticide resistance.

| ![][image2] |
| :---- |
| **Figure 2\. Gene-set enrichment analysis.** Gene-set enrichment among genes over-expressed in pirimiphos-methyl survivors relative to unexposed controls, for (A) *An. gambiae* and (B) *An. coluzzii* field-derived strains from Bouaké, Côte d’Ivoire. GO terms, PFAM domains and KEGG pathways were tested with the hypergeometric test; genes with adjusted *P* \< 0.05 and fold changes \> 1.5 were classed as over-expressed. Terms that share genes were merged into clusters (for example ABC\_tran, ABC\_membrane, aga02010 and GO:0042626 into ABC transporters), and each bar gives the best adjusted *P* among the terms in a cluster, so that one gene set is not counted several times. Every cluster is shown for both species: hollow bars are clusters that are not significant in that species, drawn at their value, and the dashed line marks an adjusted *P* of 0.05. The terms in each cluster are listed in Supplementary Table XXX. |

In *An. gambiae*, enrichment analysis pointed to two dominant signals (Figure 2). The first is ABC transporters: the ABC transporter domain (ABC\_tran; padj \= 1.4 × 10⁻⁹) and the KEGG ABC transporters pathway (aga02010; padj \= 1.5 × 10⁻³) were enriched among overexpressed genes, alongside the broader categories of transmembrane transport (GO:0055085; padj \= 3.5 × 10⁻¹²) and transmembrane transporter activity (GO:0022857; padj \= 1.2 × 10⁻⁸). The second, and the strongest signal overall, is a chitin-binding domain (CBM\_14; padj \= 7.4 × 10⁻²⁰), found in cuticular and peritrophic-matrix proteins. Ubiquitin, Hsp90 and aminopeptidase domains were also enriched, as was protein processing in the endoplasmic reticulum (aga04141; padj \= 3.3 × 10⁻⁴), which adds a proteostasis element. Many of these terms draw on the same genes, so Figure 2 merges them into clusters; even so, the transport and cuticular signals stand out as the most significant. Together they fit a response in which survivors limit how much insecticide enters or stays in the body as well as metabolising it, a possibility we return to for *ABCH1* below.

In contrast, *An. coluzzii* displayed a distinct profile, with enrichment dominated by olfactory-related categories (Figure 2). The most significant olfactory signals were the pheromone/general odorant-binding protein domain (PBP\_GOBP; padj \= 6.9 × 10⁻⁸) and GO terms for odorant binding (GO:0005549; padj \= 7.0 × 10⁻⁷), sensory perception of smell (GO:0007608; padj \= 6.9 × 10⁻⁶) and olfactory behaviour (GO:0042048; padj \= 5.9 × 10⁻³). The two phthalate-binding terms that also reached significance (padj \= 1.1 × 10⁻³) are annotations of these same proteins. The single most significant term was DUF753 (padj \= 9.5 × 10⁻¹⁶), a domain of unknown function. Odorant-binding proteins were also overexpressed in *An. gambiae* survivors (17 genes), but not enough to give a significant enrichment, so the olfactory signature is stronger in *An. coluzzii* rather than exclusive to it. Because odorant-binding proteins bind small hydrophobic molecules, one possibility is that they help to sequester the insecticide, which would need functional testing.

**Differential expression** 

Comparison of *An. gambiae* survivors with unexposed controls from Bouaké revealed a strong metabolic resistance signature centred on cytochrome P450s and carboxylesterases. Three members of the CYP6M cluster were highly overexpressed in survivors — CYP6M2 (FC \= 3.42; *padj* \= 0.000), CYP6M3 (FC \= 2.23; *padj* \= 0.000), and CYP6M4 (FC \= 2.00; *padj* \= 0.000) — implicating this locus as a contributor to pirimiphos‑methyl detoxification. These enzymes have previously been associated with both organophosphate and pyrethroid metabolism (ref?).

Several esterases also showed significant transcriptional changes \- COEAE3G (FC \= 2.29; *padj* \= 0.000) and COEAE7G (FC \= 1.80; *padj* \= 0.049) were upregulated, while COEBE1C (FC \= 0.27; *padj* \= 0.002) and COEBE3C (FC \= 0.42; *padj* \= 0.005) were downregulated. This contrasting expression within the esterase superfamily suggests divergent functional roles, with specific α‑esterases potentially enhancing detoxification capacity while reduced β‑esterase expression may reflect metabolic trade‑offs.

A strong fivefold increase in SAP2 expression (FC \= 5.03; *padj* \= 0.000) was also detected, consistent with previous evidence implicating this protein in xenobiotic sequestration and multi‑insecticide resistance. Other detoxification genes, including CYP9K1 (FC \= 0.69; *padj* \= 0.099) and Ace1 (FC \= 1.12; *padj* \= 0.769), showed no significant differential expression, indicating that their roles in resistance are likely mediated by structural variants rather than transcriptional regulation.

**Ancestry**

To investigate the genetic ancestry of our samples, we utilized ancestry informative markers (AIMs) that distinguish between *An. gambiae* and *An. coluzzii* ancestry. The analysis revealed clear species-specific patterns consistent with morphological field identifications (Figure 3A; Supplementary Table 1).

The Bouaké field samples showed high species fidelity. Samples morphologically identified as *An. gambiae* exhibited predominantly *An. gambiae* ancestry, with control samples showing 99% *An. gambiae* ancestry and only 1% *An. coluzzii* ancestry. This pattern was maintained in pirimiphos-methyl survivors (98% *An. gambiae*, 2% *An. coluzzii*). Similarly, *An. coluzzii* field samples displayed primarily *An. coluzzii* ancestry, with control samples showing 88% *An. coluzzii* and 12% *An. gambiae* ancestry, and PM-survivors showing 89% *An. coluzzii* and 11% *An. gambiae* ancestry. These minor levels of heterospecific ancestry (11-12% in *An. coluzzii*, 1-2% in *An. gambiae*) likely reflect either poorly performing AIMs, or in the case of *An. coluzzii*, the introgression of the *Vgsc-*995F F1 haplotype from *An. gambiae* into *An. coluzzii* [(Clarkson et al. 2014\)](https://paperpile.com/c/S8IWm4/bjRq). 

The laboratory reference strain Ngousso (expected to be *An. coluzzii*) showed the expected pattern with 94% *An. coluzzii* ancestry and minimal *An. gambiae* ancestry (6%). However, the Kisumu reference strain, assumed to be *An. gambiae*, exhibited an unexpected ancestry profile, with only 64% *An. gambiae* ancestry and 36% *An. coluzzii* ancestry. This *An. coluzzii* ancestry was restricted to the autosomes, whereas the X chromosome, which contains the majority of AIMs, harboured *An. gambiae* ancestry*.* This substantial proportion of *An. coluzzii* ancestry in Kisumu, a strain established from Kenya where *An. coluzzii* has not been recorded, likely indicates laboratory contamination through inadvertent hybridization during decades of colony maintenance [(Nagi et al. 2023\)](https://paperpile.com/c/S8IWm4/6hoc).

**Karyotyping** 

Chromosomal inversions are structural rearrangements where a segment of chromosome is reversed end-to-end, suppressing recombination in heterozygotes and allowing linked alleles to be inherited together as a unit. In *Anopheles* mosquitoes, inversions are associated with ecological adaptation and insecticide resistance. We examined the frequencies of two major,  ancient chromosomal inversions, 2La and 2Rb, using karyotype-tagging SNPs (Figure 3B; Supplementary Table 2).

For the 2La inversion, *An. gambiae* field samples exhibited moderate to high inversion frequencies, with control samples harboring an average of 44% inverted alleles and PM-survivors showing 48% inverted alleles (P \= 0.708, Welch’s T test). In contrast, *An. coluzzii* showed lower 2La inversion frequencies, with 36% inverted alleles in control samples decreasing to 29% in PM-survivors, though this difference was not significant (P \= 0.298, Welch’s T test). The laboratory strains showed contrasting patterns: Kisumu carried 25% inverted 2La alleles, while Ngousso showed only 12%.

The 2Rb inversion displayed more variable patterns. In *An. gambiae*, inverted alleles were present at 37% frequency in controls and at 29% in PM-survivors  (P \= 0.206). *An. coluzzii* showed a more pronounced decrease, from 15% inverted alleles in controls to just 6% in PM-survivors  (P \= 0.006), which could suggest potential negative selection against the 2Rb inversion under pirimiphos-methyl exposure in this species. The reference strains showed similar patterns to 2La, with Kisumu harboring 28% inverted 2Rb alleles and Ngousso showing minimal frequency (2%).

**Variants of interest**  
We explored the frequency of known insecticide resistance-associated alleles within each sample, and visualised these data as a heatmap, displaying the mean frequency for each treatment cohorts (Figure 3C).

The *Ace1*\-G280S mutation was at high frequencies in all Bouaké field cohorts (\>=77%) and showed an increase in frequency between unexposed controls and PM-survivors individuals in both *An. coluzzii* (77% \-\> 93%) and *An. gambiae* (94% \-\> 98%), replicating its known role in pirimiphos-methyl resistance. The *Coeae1f-*E477V mutation, associated with a selective sweep in *An. gambiae* [(Nagi *et al.*, 2024\)](https://paperpile.com/c/S8IWm4/TTx5), was found at 40% frequency in *An. gambiae* Bouaké controls and at 43% in the PM-survivor group. 

The recently described *Cyp6p3-*E205D mutation [(Kengne-Ouafo *et al.*, 2024\)](https://paperpile.com/c/S8IWm4/Z6eZ) was found at high frequencies in Bouaké *An. gambiae* (29%-40%), and low frequencies in *An. coluzzii*, whilst the *Cyp9k1*\-N224I mutation was found solely in *An. gambiae* (8-9%). *Cyp9k1*\-N224I residue forms part of the opening of the *Cyp9k1* substrate channel, potentially modulating how insecticides can reach the active site, and is associated with a selective sweep in field *An. gambiae [(Nagi et al., 2025a)](https://paperpile.com/c/S8IWm4/vybf)*. The *Cyp4j5*\-L43F mutation has previously been associated with pyrethroid resistance, however, it is strongly linked to the inverted form of the 2La inversion, and is likely to be acting as a proxy for inversion frequencies. 

At *Gste2*, we find species-specific patterns with *Gste2-*L119V predominating in *An. gambiae* (67-77%) compared to *Gste2*\-I114T (30-50%) and *Gste2-*F120L (25-37%) in *An. coluzzii*. All three mutations are located proximally to the substrate binding channel of the protein and are associated with selective sweeps in *Anopheles gambiae s.l* [(Nagi *et al.*, 2025a)](https://paperpile.com/c/S8IWm4/vybf). I114T and L119V have been associated with resistance to multiple insecticides (refs). 

At the *Voltage-gated sodium channel*, we find both the 995F (44-58%) and 402L/1527T (35-43%) haplotypes in *An. coluzzii* at moderate frequencies. In *An. gambiae*, we find L995F at almost fixation, in agreement with data from whole-genome sequencing studies (ref). We find a plethora of secondary mutations at the *Vgsc* at low frequencies (T791M, N1570Y, A1746S, P1874S/L, I1940T), which are likely to be found on the background of the F1 995F haplotype [(Clarkson et al. 2021\)](https://paperpile.com/c/S8IWm4/9150). In *An. coluzzii*, we also detect a mutation at codon 1529, F1529C, equivalent to position 1534 in *Musca domestica* codon numbering. In *Aedes aegypti,* the equivalent substitution, F1534C, has spread widely and confers resistance to pyrethroids (refs), suggesting that *Vgsc-*F1529C is also likely to be protective against pyrethroids in *Anopheles*. F1529C was detected in four of the eight *An. coluzzii* samples, at a mean read frequency of 4% in unexposed controls and 12% in survivors, and was absent from *An. gambiae* and from both laboratory strains (Supplementary Figure 2A). With four samples per group we do not test for a difference, and since *Vgsc* is not the target of pirimiphos-methyl we do not interpret this as a response to exposure. In the reads, 1529C was always found with I1527T (Supplementary Figure 1). To establish which haplotypes carry F1529C we used *An. coluzzii* whole-genome data from the MalariaGEN Ag3 resource, which does not include Bouaké. All 200 F1529C carriers among 7,287 genotyped *An. coluzzii* also carried I1527T. Of 3,566 phased 1527T haplotypes in which the F1529C state could be resolved, 154 carried 1529C, and all but five of these (149; 97%) also carried 402L, so the haplotype is a triple mutant (402L, 1527T, 1529C). V402L is the product of two independent substitutions at the same nucleotide (G>T and G>C, both encoding leucine), which segregate on separate haplotypes. F1529C occurs on both, on the G>C form in 110 haplotypes and on the G>T form in 39, and is over-represented on the G>C form (71%, against 16% of 1527T haplotypes without 1529C; Supplementary Figure 2B). One SNP 8.2 kb upstream of codon 1529 separates the two lineages: 86% of non-carrier haplotypes on the G>T background carry one allele, against 1% of those on the G>C background. None of the 154 1529C haplotypes carry the G>T lineage’s allele, including the 39 that carry 402L G>T (Supplementary Figure 2C). The simplest explanation is that 1529C arose once on the G>C haplotype and reached the G>T background by recombination at codon 402, although independent origins cannot be excluded. F1529C is also present in Ag3 *An. coluzzii* from other West African countries, where it was rare before 2019; its geographic and temporal distribution will be described elsewhere.

The lab susceptible strains also contained some insecticide resistance alleles. Both Kisumu and Ngousso almost fixed for resistance haplotypes at the *Gste2* gene; Kisumu harbors *Gste2-*I114T at (82%) alongside *Gste2-*F120L (18%), whilst Ngousso was found to contain *Gste2-*I114T at 99% frequency. The *Rdl*\-A296S was also found in Ngousso at a frequency of 41%. It is unclear whether these mutations have arisen due to laboratory contamination or natural processes. As *Gste2* and *Rdl* confer resistance to DDT and dieldrin respectively, insecticides that were used historically, it is possible that the strains contained these mutations at the time of laboratory colonisation. 

**An ABC transporter under selection: *ABCH1***

The enrichment of ABC transporters in *An. gambiae* (Figure 2\) prompted us to ask which individual transporters drive the signal, and whether any of them show evidence of selection in wild populations. Of the 24 ABC genes that were significantly differentially expressed in *An. gambiae* PM-survivors, 20 were overexpressed, against 5 of 12 in *An. coluzzii* (Fisher’s exact *P* \= 0.02), so the response in *An. gambiae* is strikingly one-sided. The overexpressed genes were not scattered at random. Ten of the 20 lie on chromosome arm 3R, and eight of those sit in two tandem arrays: four *ABCC* genes at 10.7 Mb (*ABCC9*–*ABCC11* and AGAP028128; log₂ fold changes 0.9–2.3) and four *ABCG* genes at 34 Mb (*ABCG8*, *ABCG10*, *ABCG11* and *ABCG20*). As a group the overexpressed genes lay far closer together than expected (median nearest-neighbour distance 19 kb against 1.4 Mb expected; adjusted *P* \= 0.008), so whole transporter arrays are being turned up together, which points to shared regulation or shared copy-number variation; we have not tested for either. We cross-referenced each overexpressed gene against H12 selection signals from the MalariaGEN selection atlas, restricted to West African *An. gambiae* and *An. coluzzii* cohorts. As a set, the overexpressed ABC genes were not enriched for sweep overlap once tandem arrays were collapsed into independent loci (12 loci, 3 overlapping a sweep; permutation *P* \= 0.27; odds ratio 1.7), so we do not claim a family-wide association with selection. The *ABCC* array at 10.7 Mb lies within the broad interval of a sweep signal in one Côte d’Ivoire cohort, but not at its centre. One gene stood out individually: *ABCH1* is the only ABC gene whose sweep signal is centred on the gene itself.

*ABCH1* (AGAP002638) was overexpressed in PM-survivors of both species — 2.3-fold in *An. gambiae* (*padj* \= 3.9 × 10⁻¹⁴) and 1.7-fold in *An. coluzzii* (*padj* \= 5.9 × 10⁻⁵) — and, in *An. gambiae* only, was already elevated 1.8-fold in unexposed Bouaké controls relative to the susceptible Kisumu strain (*padj* \< 10⁻⁴; Figure 4A). *An. gambiae* therefore carries both a constitutive and an inducible component at this locus, amounting to a roughly fourfold difference between survivors and the susceptible reference, whereas *An. coluzzii* shows induction alone. This mirrors the bioassay result, in which *An. gambiae* was the more resistant of the two species (34% versus 81% mortality).

The *ABCH1* locus also carries a replicated selective sweep in wild *An. coluzzii*, supported by three haplotype-based statistics. Eight Ag3 cohorts sampled between 2011 and 2018 in Burkina Faso, Mali and Ghana show an H12 signal spanning the gene, and in five of these — Comoé and Houet provinces in Burkina Faso, sampled across five years — the fitted peak focus falls on the gene itself (Figure 4B). Local H12 reaches 0.26–0.45 against a genome-wide median of 0.02–0.04 in the same cohorts. G123, which is computed from unphased genotypes and so does not depend on the haplotype phasing, places the locus (not shown) between the 99.8th and 100th percentile genome-wide in every cohort, at two to five times the genome-wide 99th percentile; iHS places it between the 96.7th and 99.8th percentile. Genome-wide, this degree of replication places the locus in the top 1.4% of genes; the most strongly swept loci in the same analysis are the canonical resistance genes *Cyp6aa1*/*Cyp6p*, the *Gste* cluster and *Cyp9k1*, which return signals in 25–33 cohorts.

The causal target of this sweep cannot be resolved from haplotype data alone. The H12 apex is tightly reproducible across cohorts (24,854,314–24,862,006 bp; median 24,856,722 bp) but sits approximately 8 kb downstream of *ABCH1*, between two odorant receptor genes, *Or39* (AGAP002639) and *Or38* (AGAP002640) (Figure 4B, lower track). An offset of this size is well within the resolution of a haplotype-based scan, so *ABCH1* is not excluded. Two observations favour it. First, neither odorant receptor is appreciably transcribed in these samples — mean normalised expression 6.7 for *Or39* and 1.8 for *Or38*, against 1,719 for *ABCH1* — and neither responds to pirimiphos-methyl exposure in either species. Second, *ABCH1* is the only gene in the interval that is differentially expressed at all. We therefore regard *ABCH1* as the most plausible candidate at this locus while noting that fine-mapping, or a functional test, would be required to establish it.

Clustering *ABCH1* haplotypes resolves the architecture of the signal and shows that it is confined to one species. Among 5,804 haplotypes from West African *An. coluzzii* (n \= 3,790) and *An. gambiae* (n \= 2,014), 663 fall into a single group within which haplotypes differ at less than 0.5% of sites; the next largest group contains 42. On a neighbour-joining tree this group forms one tight clade (Figure 4C, D). Every one of its 663 haplotypes is *An. coluzzii* — 356 from Burkina Faso, 147 from Ghana, 127 from Mali and 33 from Côte d'Ivoire — and it accounts for 17% of *An. coluzzii* haplotypes, whereas the largest *An. gambiae* group contains 30 haplotypes, or 1.5%. The swept haplotype is present in the Bouaké population itself: 22% of *An. coluzzii* haplotypes from Gbéké, the district containing Bouaké, fall in the swept clade, the highest frequency of any Ivorian cohort, against 0 of 24 *An. gambiae* haplotypes from the same district. The locus therefore carries a single swept haplotype that has spread across West Africa in *An. coluzzii*, rather than several independent sweeps, and *An. gambiae* carries no comparable swept haplotype. This mirrors the selection atlas, in which 8 of 22 West African *An. coluzzii* cohorts show a signal spanning *ABCH1* against 0 of 16 *An. gambiae* cohorts (Fisher's exact *P* \= 0.0065), despite the *An. gambiae* cohorts carrying detectable sweeps elsewhere in the genome. Copy number does not contribute: *ABCH1* is present at two copies in 3,991 of 3,997 samples, so the gene amplification that drives selection at several other detoxification loci in *An. gambiae s.l.* is absent here.

*ABCH1* is a plausible resistance gene on mechanistic grounds. ABCH transporters are restricted to arthropods and are required for cuticular hydrocarbon deposition and barrier formation in insects, so elevated expression could reduce the rate at which insecticide penetrates the cuticle rather than acting through metabolism or efflux of the compound itself. This is consistent with the cuticular and chitin-binding categories that also emerged from the *An. gambiae* enrichment analysis (Figure 2). We note that the sweep is observed in *An. coluzzii* cohorts whereas the stronger expression phenotype is in *An. gambiae*, and cross-population haplotype homozygosity (H1X) between sympatric *An. coluzzii* and *An. gambiae* in Burkina Faso does not reach the genome-wide 99th percentile at this locus, so the swept haplotype does not appear to be shared between the two species by introgression. The Bouaké samples themselves are also not in Ag3, so the selection and expression evidence are drawn from different populations.

Finally, we asked whether the odorant-binding proteins showed a comparable signature. They did not: of 75 OBPs, none overlapped an H12 peak focus in any West African cohort and only two fell within a broader signal interval. The chemosensory response in Bouaké therefore appears to be transcriptional, with no detectable footprint of recent positive selection at these genes.

# **Discussion**

Pirimiphos-methyl is one of the few insecticides that can still be sprayed indoors against pyrethroid-resistant malaria vectors, and mosquitoes are beginning to survive it. We asked how, by comparing the transcriptomes of survivors and unexposed controls in two sibling species living side by side in the same Ivorian villages. The answer depends on the species. *An. gambiae*, the more resistant of the two, turned up cytochrome P450s, carboxylesterases, ABC transporters and cuticular proteins, whereas *An. coluzzii*, which was less resistant, showed a quieter response dominated by odorant-binding proteins. Only one gene, the ABC transporter *ABCH1*, was overexpressed in survivors of both species, and it sits at a selective sweep that has spread through wild *An. coluzzii* across West Africa. Resistance to a single insecticide is therefore not a single phenomenon even within a species complex, and a surveillance programme that pools the two species will blur part of the picture.

The target-site mutation *Ace1*-G280S is the obvious place to start, and the data confirm it matters: its frequency rose in survivors of both species, from 77% to 93% in *An. coluzzii* and from 94% to 98% in *An. gambiae*. It cannot be the whole explanation. In *An. gambiae* the allele was already near fixation in unexposed mosquitoes, yet two-thirds survived the assay, so something other than the allele must separate survivors from the rest; in *An. coluzzii* it was still below fixation in survivors. The genes overexpressed in *An. gambiae* survivors point to candidates. *CYP6M2*, *CYP6M3* and *CYP6M4* sit in a cluster whose members metabolise pyrethroids and, in the case of *CYP6M2*, can also act on organophosphates (ref). Whether such activity protects or harms is a genuine open question, because P450s can convert organophosphates into their more toxic oxons as readily as into harmless products, and overexpression of *CYP6M2* has been reported to increase susceptibility to malathion (ref). That the P450s are higher in the animals that lived is more consistent with protection, but this needs enzymatic and functional work. The same applies to the α-esterases *COEAE3G* and *COEAE7G*, which could sequester oxons before they reach acetylcholinesterase, and to the sensory appendage protein *SAP2*, whose fivefold increase fits its reported role in insecticide sequestration (ref). Notably, the E477V variant at the *Coeae1f* duplication that drives pirimiphos-methyl resistance elsewhere in West Africa (ref) showed no clear rise in survivors (40% to 43%), although with four pools per group we could not detect a modest change.

Any comparison of survivors with unexposed controls carries a limitation: survivors were exposed and controls were not, so part of what separates them is the physiological response to the insecticide rather than inherited resistance. Two observations suggest that at least part of the signal is heritable. *ABCH1* was already elevated in unexposed Bouaké *An. gambiae* relative to the susceptible Kisumu strain, although a laboratory strain differs from wild mosquitoes in many ways, and the gene lies at a sweep in wild *An. coluzzii*, which marks selection on heritable variation at the locus. Other differences should be read as candidates until they are tied to genotype.

The ABC transporters illustrate both the promise and the risk of enrichment analysis. In *An. gambiae*, 20 of the 24 differentially expressed ABC genes were upregulated, and they were not scattered: eight sit in two tandem arrays on chromosome 3R, an *ABCC* array and an *ABCG* array whose members are raised together. Arrays that move together suggest shared regulation or shared copy-number variation, both of which are testable and neither of which we have tested. As a family, though, these genes were not enriched for selective sweeps once each array was counted as one locus, so we do not claim that ABC transporters in general have been targeted by selection. Against that background, *ABCH1* is striking. It is the only ABC gene whose sweep is centred on the gene, the sweep is replicated in eight cohorts from three countries and supported by H12, G123 and iHS, and the swept haplotype is a single clade that accounts for 17% of *An. coluzzii* haplotypes in the region. ABCH transporters occur only in arthropods and are needed to lay down cuticular hydrocarbons, so more of them could slow the passage of a contact insecticide through the cuticle (ref). This would sit well with the enrichment of chitin-binding proteins in *An. gambiae* survivors, and with growing evidence that cuticular changes contribute to resistance in *Anopheles* (refs), but it remains a hypothesis.

The most puzzling feature of the *ABCH1* result is that the sweep is in *An. coluzzii* whereas the stronger expression phenotype is in *An. gambiae*. Several readings are possible and they are not mutually exclusive. The sweep apex lies about 8 kb from the gene, between two odorant receptors, which is where a regulatory variant could sit; if so, the swept haplotype might increase *ABCH1* expression in *An. coluzzii* in a way we cannot see, because the Bouaké mosquitoes were not whole-genome sequenced and are absent from Ag3. *An. gambiae* may reach higher expression by a different route, and the swept haplotype does not appear to have crossed between species, since cross-population haplotype homozygosity between them is unremarkable at this locus. Or the gene may be under selection for something other than pirimiphos-methyl; pyrethroids have been used in West Africa for much longer, and cuticle function matters for water balance as well as insecticide uptake. The experiment that would separate these is simple: genotype Bouaké *An. coluzzii* at the swept haplotype and ask whether carriers express more *ABCH1*.

Odorant-binding proteins are the other signature worth reflecting on. They were enriched among genes overexpressed in *An. coluzzii* survivors, but they were also raised in *An. gambiae*, and none of the 75 odorant-binding protein genes overlaps a sweep, so this is a response without an evident genetic basis. Because these proteins bind small hydrophobic molecules, sequestration of the insecticide is conceivable. So is a behavioural effect, in which altered olfaction changes how long a mosquito stays on a treated surface, and the transcriptomes of survivors might then partly reflect behaviour rather than physiology. The lower frequency of the 2Rb inversion in surviving *An. coluzzii* is likewise a lead rather than a result: it rests on three or four pools per group and was not corrected for multiple testing.

Finally, we detected the F1529C substitution in the voltage-gated sodium channel of *An. coluzzii*, equivalent to F1534C in *Aedes aegypti*, where it contributes to pyrethroid resistance (ref). The sodium channel is not the target of pirimiphos-methyl, and we do not think its presence reflects the exposure, but it is a reminder that these mosquitoes have been selected by many insecticides and that RNA-seq can reveal target-site variation as well as expression. In Ag3, F1529C sits on haplotypes that carry both I1527T and V402L, and the arrangement of the two independent V402L lineages is most simply explained by a single origin on the V402L G>C haplotype followed by recombination, although independent origins cannot be excluded. How F1529C has spread across West Africa, and whether it confers pyrethroid resistance in *Anopheles*, will be described elsewhere.

Our conclusions are limited by design. Each group comprised four pools of five mosquitoes, so effects of modest size will be missed and the chance of spurious findings in the smaller sets, such as the karyotype comparisons, is real. The mosquitoes were F1 progeny reared in the laboratory, which reduces environmental variation but may also change expression. The selection evidence comes from populations other than Bouaké, and no finding here has yet been tested functionally. Within those limits, the results say where to look next. Gene editing or RNAi of *ABCH1*, with bioassays and cuticular hydrocarbon profiling, would test the cuticle hypothesis. Whole-genome sequencing of Bouaké mosquitoes would show whether the swept haplotype is present and whether it tracks expression. And transporter and cuticular genes deserve a place beside *Ace1* and the esterases in studies of how resistance to pirimiphos-methyl evolves, now that clothianidin is entering use and keeping organophosphates effective matters more than ever.

# **Materials and Methods**

**Sample collections and phenotyping**  
Sampling in Côte d’Ivoire was performed in June-July 2019 from the villages of Abroko (7.89⁰N, 5.09⁰W), Kologonouan (7.83⁰N, 5.08⁰W), and Konzo (7.49⁰N, 5.07⁰W), located within the Gbêkê region of central Côte d’Ivoire, close to the city of Bouaké. Blood-fed female mosquitoes were collected by Prokopack aspiration with those identified as *Anopheles* held in paper drinking cups containing a filter paper circle at the base with a damp cotton wool pad underneath until egg deposition. Filter papers with eggs were packaged individually in sealed plastic bags and sent by courier to LSTM. Eggs were floated as isofemale batches in individual paper cups containing water, and upon hatching a pinch of finely ground Tetramin was added daily. Upon development to the third larval instar stage, six larvae were removed and pooled and DNA was extracted by boiling in TE buffer and used for species identification (Santolamazza et al. 2008).

After the identification of the species, only families containing solely *An. gambiae* or *An. coluzzii* were retained and upon pupation, families from each species were pooled into single-species cages and reared to adults for pirimiphos-methyl bioassays using 3-5 day-old females in the standard WHO tube test protocol (0.25% p-methyl paper; 60 min exposure; mortality recorded after 24h; WHO 2016). All rearing and testing was performed at ≈25⁰C and 80% relative humidity, with control females exposed to untreated paper. Bioassay survivors and unexposed controls were stored in Eppendorf tubes at \-80 C for later RNA extraction. The lab-susceptible strains Kisumu (*An. gambiae*, Kenya) and Ngousso (*An. coluzzii*, Cameroon) were used as a second comparator group for each species.

**RNA-Sequencing**  
Total RNA was extracted from pools of five females using the PicoPure RNA isolation kit (Thermo Fisher Scientific) according to the manufacturer’s protocol. Total RNA extracted from mosquitoes was treated using DNase (RNase free DNase set, Qiagen Hilden Germany). The concentration and quality of the extracted RNA were evaluated using a NanoDrop spectrophotometer (Thermo Fisher Scientific) and an Agilent Tapestation 2200 using high‐sensitivity RNA screentape. Total RNA was also extracted from pools of two standard insecticide susceptible laboratory colonies Kisumu (*An. gambiae*) and Ngousso (*An. coluzzii*). Four biological replicate pools (each from N=5 mosquitoes) were sent to Novogene, where libraries were enriched for mRNA using a poly-A enrichment method, and sequenced on an Illumina NovaSeq.

**Data analysis**

All data analyses were performed using the RNA-Seq-Pop workflow [(Nagi *et al.*, 2023\)](https://paperpile.com/c/S8IWm4/6hoc), a comprehensive Snakemake pipeline for RNA sequencing analysis. Raw sequencing reads were processed through quality control using FastQC [(Andrews, 2010\)](https://paperpile.com/c/S8IWm4/O0Q0), with adapter sequences removed using fastp [(Chen *et al.*, 2018\)](https://paperpile.com/c/S8IWm4/Qc8l) and quality metrics integrated using MultiQC [(Ewels *et al.*, 2016\)](https://paperpile.com/c/S8IWm4/Fd4z). For differential expression analysis, trimmed reads were aligned to the *An. gambiae* AgamP4.12 reference transcriptome using Kallisto [(Pimentel *et al.*, 2017\)](https://paperpile.com/c/S8IWm4/r4QS), with gene-level differential expression performed using DESeq2 [(Love *et al.*, 2014\)](https://paperpile.com/c/S8IWm4/YFz0). Principal component analysis and Pearson correlation analysis were performed on DESeq2-normalized count data to assess sample relationships. Gene set enrichment analyses were performed using the hypergeometric test with the python package AnoExpress [(Nagi *et al.*, 2025b)](https://paperpile.com/c/S8IWm4/KwXp). 

For variant calling and population genetic analyses, reads were aligned to the reference genome using HISAT2 [(Kim *et al.*, 2019\)](https://paperpile.com/c/S8IWm4/3ht4), with SNPs called using FreeBayes version 1.3.2 [(Garrison *et al.*, 2012\)](https://paperpile.com/c/S8IWm4/t36I) and annotated with SnpEff version 5.0 [(Cingolani *et al.*, 2012\)](https://paperpile.com/c/S8IWm4/uxzs). Ancestry analysis used ancestry informative markers derived from the 16 genomes project [(Neafsey *et al.*, 2015\)](https://paperpile.com/c/S8IWm4/xObz), while chromosomal inversion karyotyping for 2La and 2Rb inversions was conducted using previously published tagging SNPs [(Love *et al.*, 2019\)](https://paperpile.com/c/S8IWm4/nOdn). Variant allele frequencies were calculated directly from BAM files. To visualise reads we used IGV directly on BAM files [(Robinson et al. 2011\)](https://paperpile.com/c/S8IWm4/WFYn).

**Differential expression**

Differential expression was tested with DESeq2 in four contrasts. Within each field species, pirimiphos-methyl survivors were compared with unexposed controls from Bouaké; to ask whether a gene was already elevated before exposure, unexposed Bouaké controls were compared with the susceptible laboratory strain of the same species (Kisumu for *An. gambiae*, Ngousso for *An. coluzzii*). P values were adjusted for multiple testing by the Benjamini–Hochberg procedure, genes with an adjusted P < 0.05 were called differentially expressed, and fold changes are given for survivors relative to controls (or field relative to laboratory strain). A fold-change threshold was applied only in the enrichment analysis, below.

**Gene-set enrichment**

Over-expressed genes (adjusted P < 0.05 and fold change > 1.5) were tested for enrichment of Gene Ontology terms, PFAM protein domains and KEGG pathways using a one-sided hypergeometric test, implemented in AnoExpress, with gene annotations from AnoExpress. [CHECK: background gene set; multiple-testing correction.] Terms were retained if their adjusted P < 0.05. Many terms are annotations of the same genes, so we merged terms with shared gene content into clusters (for example the ABC transporter domain, KEGG ABC transporter pathway and ATPase-coupled transport term), and plotted the best adjusted P among the terms in each cluster so that a single set of genes was not counted several times. The terms in each cluster are listed in Supplementary Table X. Only over-expressed genes were tested.

**Gene family definitions**

ABC transporters were defined as genes with the ABC transporter nucleotide-binding domain (PFAM PF00005) or a gene name beginning with *Abc* (56 genes). Odorant-binding proteins were defined as genes with the PFAM domain PF01395, the GO term GO:0005549 or a gene name containing *obp* (75 genes). An earlier, broader definition of the ABC family that included GO:0042626 and four transmembrane-domain PFAMs was abandoned because it included P-type and V-type ATPases and other ATP-binding proteins that are not ABC transporters.

**Genomic clustering of differentially expressed genes**

To test whether overexpressed genes of a family lie closer together than expected, we calculated the median distance from each gene to its nearest neighbour on the same chromosome arm; a gene with no neighbour on its arm was assigned a distance of 300 Mb. The observed median was compared with a null distribution from 10,000 draws of the same number of genes from the family, and the proportion of draws with a median as small as that observed was taken as the P value. P values were adjusted across family and species combinations by the Benjamini–Hochberg procedure.

**Overlap with selective sweeps**

All analyses of Ag3 data used only sample sets without a use restriction (`unrestricted_use` in the Ag3 sample-set table); the selection-atlas cohorts contain no restricted samples. Selective sweep signals were taken from a genome-wide scan of Ag3 cohorts with H12 (selection atlas; ref), in which each signal has an interval and a fitted peak focus. We used signals from *An. gambiae* and *An. coluzzii* cohorts sampled in West Africa (Benin, Burkina Faso, Cameroon, Côte d'Ivoire, the Gambia, Ghana, Guinea, Guinea-Bissau, Liberia, Mali, Niger, Nigeria, Senegal, Sierra Leone and Togo). A gene was counted as overlapping a sweep if its coordinates intersected the interval of a signal, and as centred on a sweep if the peak focus fell within the gene. To test whether a set of overexpressed genes overlapped sweeps more often than expected, genes lying within 200 kb of one another on the same arm were first merged into a single locus, because neighbouring genes share a signal, and the number of swept loci was compared with a null distribution from 10,000 random draws of the same number of genes from the same chromosome arms.

**Selection statistics at ABCH1**

For the cohorts with a signal spanning *ABCH1* we recomputed H12 in windows of 1,000 SNPs along chromosome arm 2R using phased haplotypes (analysis gamb_colu) from the malariagen_data package, sampling up to 50 individuals per cohort, with a minimum of 15, and a fixed random seed. G123 was calculated in windows of 1,000 SNPs from unphased genotypes, and iHS from phased haplotypes, standardised and summarised in windows of 200 SNPs. For each statistic we report the percentile of the locus among all windows genome-wide in the same cohort. The population branch statistic (PBS) was calculated in 10 kb windows with at least 40 segregating sites, as PBS = (T(A,B) + T(A,C) − T(B,C))/2, where T = −log(1 − F_ST) and F_ST is Hudson's estimator, computed as a ratio of averages within each window. The focal population A was each *An. coluzzii* cohort, B was *An. gambiae* from the same country, and C was *An. arabiensis* from Burkina Faso as the outgroup. Cross-population haplotype homozygosity (H1X) was calculated between *An. coluzzii* and *An. gambiae* from Burkina Faso in 1,000-SNP windows. Gene copy number at *ABCH1* was taken from the modal copy-number state of the Ag3 gene copy-number calls for *An. coluzzii* from the four countries, excluding samples with coverage variance above 0.2.

**Haplotype clustering**

Phased biallelic SNPs within *ABCH1* (2R:24,825,285–24,848,323) were extracted from *An. coluzzii* and *An. gambiae* from Burkina Faso, Mali, Ghana and Côte d'Ivoire, sampling at random up to 40 individuals per cohort (admin2 unit and year). Pairwise Hamming distances were computed from the haplotype matrix, and haplotypes were clustered by complete linkage, with groups defined by cutting the tree at a distance of 0.5% of sites. The same distance matrix was used to build a neighbour-joining tree with the anjl package. 

**Statistics**

Inversion frequencies were compared between survivors and controls with Welch's t-test across samples, without correction for the number of comparisons. Fisher's exact test was used for comparisons of counts. Analyses were run in Python in a pixi-managed environment; code is available at https://github.com/sanjaynagi/bouake-pm-transcriptomics.

**Vgsc haplotype background**

To establish which haplotypes carry F1529C we used *An. coluzzii* in the MalariaGEN Ag3 resource (malariagen\_data Python package), restricted to sample sets whose terms of use allow unrestricted use (`unrestricted_use` in the Ag3 sample-set table); sets still under a use restriction were excluded. Genotypes at *Vgsc* codons 402, 1527 and 1529 (transcript AGAP004707-RD) were identified by nucleotide: V402L as G>T or G>C at 2L:2,391,228 (G>A, which encodes V402I, was not counted), I1527T as T>C at 2L:2,429,617 and F1529C as T>G at 2L:2,429,623. The Ag3 phased haplotypes (*gamb\_colu* analysis) are biallelic and omit V402L and F1529C, so each V402L substitution was phased onto the surrounding phased scaffold with a copying-model method developed for the selection atlas (ref), which compares the two haplotypes of each heterozygote against the other carriers and non-carriers in a window of 1,500 scaffold SNPs; a site is declined if more than 2% of its heterozygotes cannot be separated or if it shows an excess of heterozygotes. Both V402L substitutions passed (0.05% and 0% of heterozygotes tied). F1529C was declined (34% of 180 heterozygotes tied), so haplotypes were assigned from copy number: because every carrier also carried I1527T, 1529C was placed on every 1527T haplotype of a sample when the sample's 1529C copy number equalled its number of 1527T haplotypes, on none when it was zero, and the sample was excluded otherwise. To ask whether 1529C arose separately on the two 402L backgrounds, the SNP within 25 kb of codon 1529 that best separated non-carrier haplotypes on the G>T and G>C backgrounds (150 sampled per background) was identified using non-carriers only, and the frequency of the G>T lineage's allele was then tabulated in the 1529C haplotypes, which were not used to choose it. Scripts are in the project repository (analysis/f1529c).

**Data availability**  
Raw sequencing data have been deposited in the Sequence Read Archive (SRA) under BioProject accession PRJNA1134421.  
Analysis code, manuscript figure scripts and result tables are available at https://github.com/sanjaynagi/bouake-pm-transcriptomics.
